Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2)

﴿By the declining day (al-'Asr)﴾ [1] ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [2] ﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience﴾ [3].

God Almighty swore by al-'Asr with an oath intended to confirm the statement, as is the way of the oaths of the Qur'an.

That by which the oath is sworn is among the manifestations of the wondrous Divine creation, which point to the greatness of His power and the vastness of His knowledge.

The word al-'Asr has several meanings. What is meant by it can only be a state that points to one of the attributes of the Divine acts. It is determined either by an implied annexation (idafa), or by a contextual indication, or by prior reference (ahd). Whatever is meant by it here, the oath by it is because it is a time that recalls the great power of God Almighty in creating the world and its conditions, and recalls great blessed matters, such as the particular prayer, or a specific blessed era.

The best-known use of the word al-'Asr is as a proper name, by predominant usage, for a certain time between the end of the time of Zuhr and the yellowing of the sun. Its beginning is when the shadow of an object becomes equal to its height, in addition to the amount of shadow it had at the sun's zenith. It extends until the shadow of an object becomes twice its height, in addition to the shadow it had at the sun's zenith. That is the time of the sun's yellowing. al-'Asr is the beginning of the late afternoon ('ashiyy). It is followed by the early evening (asil) and the reddening, which is the time before sunset. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"She sensed a faint sound, and the hunter frightened her, in the late afternoon, when the evening had drawn near."

That is a time that announces the nearness of the end of the day. It recalls the creation of the sun and the earth, and the order of the earth's movement around the sun, the movement from which night and day come about each day. From this angle it is like the oath by the forenoon (duha), by the night and the day, and by the dawn, all of them atmospheric states that change with the change in the direction of the sun's rays toward the globe of the earth.

At that time people prepare to stop their daytime work, such as tending their fields and gardens and their trade in the markets. So it recalls the wisdom of the order of human society, and the diligence in work and the order for beginning and ending it that God inspired in human instinct. In it people hasten toward their homes to spend the night and to enjoy the company of their families and children. This is part of the blessing (ni'ma) or of bliss (na'im). It also hints at a reminder of the likeness of life, when people's appointed terms draw near after the stages of youth, middle age and old age have passed.

On these interpretations, its definition with the article lam is a definition of mental reference (ahd dhihni), that is, every 'asr.

Al-'Asr is also used for the prayer fixed to the time of al-'Asr. It is an exalted prayer. It was said that it is what is meant by the "middle prayer" in the words of God Almighty: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 238]. It is reported in the hadith: ("Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property.") And it is reported in the sound hadith: ("Three to whom God will not speak on the Day of Resurrection"), and it mentions "a man who swore a false oath after 'Asr over a commodity, claiming that he had been offered for it what he had not been offered." Its definition on this reading is a definition of reference (ahd), and it became a proper name by predominant usage, as is the case with many generic nouns defined with the lam, such as al-'Aqaba.

Al-'Asr is also used for a known period of the existence of a generation of people, or a king, or a prophet, or a religion, and it is specified by annexation. One says: the age of al-Fitahl, the age of Ibrahim, the age of Iskandar (Alexander), the age of Jahiliyya. It is possible that this usage is what is meant here, and that what is meant by it is the age of the Prophet (ﷺ). The definition in it would be the definition of present reference (ahd hudhuri), like the definition in "al-yawm" in your saying: "I did such-and-such today." The oath by it would then be like the oath by his life in the words of God Almighty: (La-'amruka, "By your life"). al-Fakhr said: "So He, Exalted is He, swore by his time in this verse, by his place in His words ﴿while you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by his life in the words (La-'amruka)." End of quotation.

It is also possible that what is meant is the whole age of Islam, which is the last of the ages of the religions for this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the age of the Muslim community, in relation to the age of the Jews and the age of the Christians, to the period from the 'Asr prayer until sunset, in his words: "The likeness of the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians is that of a man who hired laborers to work for him until night. The Jews worked until midday, then said: 'We have no need of your wage, and what we have done is in vain.' He then hired others after them and said: 'Complete the rest of your day, and you shall have what I stipulated for them.' So they worked until the time of the 'Asr prayer, then said: 'What we have done is yours in vain, and the wage you set for us is yours.' Then he hired a people to work the rest of their day, and they worked until the sun set, and they received the wage of both groups together. So you are they." Perhaps that prophetic likeness is connected with the allusion to the age of Islam in this verse.

It is also possible to interpret al-'Asr in this verse as all of time. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about al-'Asr, and he said: 'Your Lord has sworn by the end of the day.'" These meanings can be covered by no word other than the word al-'Asr.

The suitability of the oath by al-'Asr to the purpose of the surah, on the reading that the age of Islam is meant, is clear. For the surah explained the condition of people in the age of Islam: between those who disbelieved in it, and those who believed and fully attained their share of the deeds that Islam brought. From it one also learns the condition of those who became Muslims but whose deeds fell short in varying degrees. As for the conditions of the nations before Islam, they differed according to the coming of messengers to some nations, and the remaining of some nations without laws, holding to something other than the religion of Islam, whether polytheism or a religion that Islam came to abrogate (naskh), such as Judaism and Christianity. God Almighty said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, never will it be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The definition of al-insan (mankind) is a generic definition intended to include all (istighraq), and it is a customary inclusion ('urfi),

because it includes the individuals of the human kind present at the time of the revelation of the verse, which is the time of the emergence of Islam, as you have just learned. It is specific to the people whom the call reached in the lands of the world, in varying degrees. Since those who believed and did righteous deeds are excepted from it, its ruling remains in force for non-believers, as will come...

Khusr (loss) is a verbal noun (masdar), the opposite of profit in trade. It is used here metaphorically for the bad outcome of one who thinks that he has a good outcome. That is the lasting outcome, namely the outcome of a human being in his Hereafter, of bliss or punishment.

This has already been discussed at the words of God Almighty: ﴿So their trade did not profit them﴾ [al-Baqara: 16] in Surat al-Baqara. Similar expressions recur in the Qur'an, both near and far.

The containment (zarfiyya) in His words ﴿is in loss﴾ is metaphorical. The constant presence of loss is likened to the enclosure of the container around what it contains, which is more eloquent than saying "Indeed mankind is losing."

The coming of this statement in general terms, together with its confirmation by an oath and by a particle of emphasis in its response, conveys dread and a warning about the state that surrounds most people.

It is followed by the exception in His words: ﴿Except for those who believe﴾ to the end of the verse. Thus the ruling is fully established in the mind of the listener, making clear that people are two groups: a group that is overtaken by loss, and a group that is not touched by any of it. Those who believed and did righteous deeds are not overtaken by loss in any case, provided they did not abandon any righteous deeds by committing their opposites, which are evil deeds.

Among the greatest righteous deeds is repentance from sins for those who commit them. Whoever has the attribute of faith and did not commit evil deeds, or committed them and repented of them, has attained the opposite of loss, which is metaphorical profit, that is, a good outcome of his affair. As for one who did not do righteous deeds and did not repent of his evil deeds, the ruling on that from which the exception is made has been realized in him, namely loss.

This loss varies in degree. The greatest and everlasting is the loss that results from the absence of belief in the oneness of God and the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). Below that, the levels of loss vary according to the abundance of evil deeds, outward and inward. What Islam has defined for this, in terms of the levels of deeds,

and the forgiveness of some minor lapses (lamam) when the one who commits them avoids the major sins and the abominations, is what was given as the interpretation of the words of God Almighty: ﴿Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114].

This statement is meant to take effect in the future, by the indication of the context of warning and threat, that is: in loss in the eternal life of the Hereafter. So no regard is to be given to people's conditions in the life of this world. God Almighty said: ﴿Let not the free movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197].

The indefiniteness (tankir) of (khusr) may be for classification (tanwi'), and it may convey magnification and generality in the context of dread and in the setting of an oath.

The meaning is: people are in great loss, and they are the polytheists.

The definition in His word (al-salihat) is a generic definition intended to include all, that is: they did all the righteous deeds that they were commanded to do by the command of the religion. Doing righteous deeds includes leaving evil deeds. The exception of those described by the content of the relative clause and what is joined to it gives an allusion to the reason for the ruling of the exception, which is the opposite of the ruling established for the one from whom the exception is made. For they are not in loss because they believed and did righteous deeds.

As for faith, it is a reality predicated of its particulars by equivalence (tawatu'). As for righteous deeds, their generality is predicated by gradation (tashkik). This points to the fact that the absence of loss from them is measured by the amount of righteous deeds they did, and in that there are many levels.

The exception of those who believed and did righteous deeds from being in loss indicates that the reason why the rest of mankind is in loss is the absence of faith and righteous deeds, by the indication of the implication of the attribute (mafhum al-sifa). It is known from the relative pronoun that faith and righteous deeds are the cause of the absence of loss enveloping a person.

Mutual advising to truth and mutual advising to patience are joined to doing righteous deeds, even though that is part of doing righteous deeds. This is the joining of the specific to the general for the sake of emphasis, because it may be overlooked, and it may be thought that a righteous deed is what only affects a person's own private conduct. So it alerts us that among the commanded deeds is a Muslim's guiding others and calling them to the truth. Mutual advising to truth includes teaching

the realities of guidance and the beliefs of what is correct, and training the self to understand them by doing what is right and leaving what is wrong.

Mutual advising to patience is joined to mutual advising to truth, again as the joining of the specific to the general, though its specificity is a partial specificity (khusus min wajh), because patience is bearing the hardship of establishing the truth and the harm that confronts a Muslim in his own person in establishing some part of the truth.

The reality of patience is that it is a person's restraining himself from obtaining what he desires, or from attempting to obtain it (if it is hard to obtain), so he gives up attempting to obtain it because of fear of harm arising from taking it, such as fear of God's anger or the punishment of those in authority, or out of desire to gain a benefit from it, such as patience in the hardship of jihad and the Hajj out of desire for reward, and patience in arduous work out of desire to gain wealth or reputation or the like.

Part of patience is bearing what a Muslim meets when he enjoins good, such as the resentment of some of those he enjoins, or their harm by word, like one who says to the one who commands him: "Why don't you look to your own affairs?" or the like.

As for bearing the hardship of doing evil, such as enduring the strain of staying up late in amusement and sins, or enduring the foul taste of wine for its drinker, it is not patience, because that endurance arises from the greater preponderance of the desire for that hardship over the dislike of the hardship that confronts him in abandoning it.

The words of the Most High, ﴿and enjoin one another to truth, and enjoin one another to patience﴾, comprise the establishment of all religious interests. The Islamic beliefs and the moral qualities of the religion fall under "truth", while righteous deeds and the avoidance of evil deeds fall under "patience".

Acquiring the character trait of patience is the foundation of all virtuous morals. For training oneself in praiseworthy morals inevitably involves compelling oneself to oppose many desires. In opposing them there is a hardship that requires patience, until noble morals become an ingrained disposition for the one who has trained his soul in them. As 'Amr ibn al-'As said:

If a man does not give up food he loves,
and does not restrain a straying heart wherever it heads,

Page 534

then it is likely that you will find in him, for all time, a disgrace,
which, when its like are mentioned, fills the mouth.

Likewise, all righteous deeds involve forcing the soul to abandon what it inclines toward. In the hadith: "Paradise is surrounded by disliked things, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Patience is a mount that never stumbles."

The discussion of patience has already been given in full at the words of the Most High: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The form of mutual enjoining (tawasi) of truth and of patience indicates that the life of the believers should be founded on the prevalence of mutual urging to both as their constant habit. That requires the believers to be characterized by upholding the truth and by their patience in the face of disliked things for the sake of the interests of Islam and its community. This is in accordance with what people's custom entails: that no one enjoins another to keep to a matter unless he considers that matter worthy of being kept to. For rarely does anyone venture to command a right which he himself does not do, or to command patience while he is impatient. The Most High said in rebuke of the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you command people to righteousness and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Will you not then use reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. This meaning has also been discussed earlier at the words of the Most High: ﴿and you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr: 18], in Surah al-Fajr.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Humazah

This surah is named in the mushafs and most tafsirs "Surat al-Humazah", with the definite article lam. In Sahih al-Bukhari and some tafsirs it is titled "Surat Wayl li-kulli Humazah". Al-Fayruzabadi mentioned in Basa'ir Dhawi al-Tamyiz that it is also called "Surat al-Hutamah", because that word occurs in it.

It is Makkan by agreement.

It is counted the thirty-second in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Qiyamah and before Surat al-Mursalat.

Its verses are nine, by agreement.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who had set themselves up to deride the Muslims, to revile them, and to fabricate evil tales about them. Among these polytheists the following were named: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Jamil ibn Ma'mar of Banu Jumah (he accepted Islam on the day of the Conquest and witnessed Hunayn), and al-'As ibn Wa'il of Banu Sahm, all of them among the chiefs of Quraysh. Also named were al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, both of Thaqif, of the chiefs of Thaqif among the people of al-Ta'if. All of these were people of wealth in the Jahiliyyah, flourishing through their riches and their nobility. The verse of the surah came in general terms, so its ruling covers those named and those like them among the polytheists whose names were not mentioned.

* * *

The purpose of this surah is a warning of punishment to a group of polytheists who made backbiting (hamz) and slandering (lamz) of the Muslims a kind of their harassment, hoping that weariness from the various kinds of harm would drive the Muslims to turn away from Islam and return to polytheism.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2)

﴿By the declining day (al-'Asr)﴾ [1] ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [2] ﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience﴾ [3].

God Almighty swore by al-'Asr with an oath intended to confirm the statement, as is the way of the oaths of the Qur'an.

That by which the oath is sworn is among the manifestations of the wondrous Divine creation, which point to the greatness of His power and the vastness of His knowledge.

The word al-'Asr has several meanings. What is meant by it can only be a state that points to one of the attributes of the Divine acts. It is determined either by an implied annexation (idafa), or by a contextual indication, or by prior reference (ahd). Whatever is meant by it here, the oath by it is because it is a time that recalls the great power of God Almighty in creating the world and its conditions, and recalls great blessed matters, such as the particular prayer, or a specific blessed era.

The best-known use of the word al-'Asr is as a proper name, by predominant usage, for a certain time between the end of the time of Zuhr and the yellowing of the sun. Its beginning is when the shadow of an object becomes equal to its height, in addition to the amount of shadow it had at the sun's zenith. It extends until the shadow of an object becomes twice its height, in addition to the shadow it had at the sun's zenith. That is the time of the sun's yellowing. al-'Asr is the beginning of the late afternoon ('ashiyy). It is followed by the early evening (asil) and the reddening, which is the time before sunset. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"She sensed a faint sound, and the hunter frightened her, in the late afternoon, when the evening had drawn near."

That is a time that announces the nearness of the end of the day. It recalls the creation of the sun and the earth, and the order of the earth's movement around the sun, the movement from which night and day come about each day. From this angle it is like the oath by the forenoon (duha), by the night and the day, and by the dawn, all of them atmospheric states that change with the change in the direction of the sun's rays toward the globe of the earth.

At that time people prepare to stop their daytime work, such as tending their fields and gardens and their trade in the markets. So it recalls the wisdom of the order of human society, and the diligence in work and the order for beginning and ending it that God inspired in human instinct. In it people hasten toward their homes to spend the night and to enjoy the company of their families and children. This is part of the blessing (ni'ma) or of bliss (na'im). It also hints at a reminder of the likeness of life, when people's appointed terms draw near after the stages of youth, middle age and old age have passed.

On these interpretations, its definition with the article lam is a definition of mental reference (ahd dhihni), that is, every 'asr.

Al-'Asr is also used for the prayer fixed to the time of al-'Asr. It is an exalted prayer. It was said that it is what is meant by the "middle prayer" in the words of God Almighty: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 238]. It is reported in the hadith: ("Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property.") And it is reported in the sound hadith: ("Three to whom God will not speak on the Day of Resurrection"), and it mentions "a man who swore a false oath after 'Asr over a commodity, claiming that he had been offered for it what he had not been offered." Its definition on this reading is a definition of reference (ahd), and it became a proper name by predominant usage, as is the case with many generic nouns defined with the lam, such as al-'Aqaba.

Al-'Asr is also used for a known period of the existence of a generation of people, or a king, or a prophet, or a religion, and it is specified by annexation. One says: the age of al-Fitahl, the age of Ibrahim, the age of Iskandar (Alexander), the age of Jahiliyya. It is possible that this usage is what is meant here, and that what is meant by it is the age of the Prophet (ﷺ). The definition in it would be the definition of present reference (ahd hudhuri), like the definition in "al-yawm" in your saying: "I did such-and-such today." The oath by it would then be like the oath by his life in the words of God Almighty: (La-'amruka, "By your life"). al-Fakhr said: "So He, Exalted is He, swore by his time in this verse, by his place in His words ﴿while you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by his life in the words (La-'amruka)." End of quotation.

It is also possible that what is meant is the whole age of Islam, which is the last of the ages of the religions for this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the age of the Muslim community, in relation to the age of the Jews and the age of the Christians, to the period from the 'Asr prayer until sunset, in his words: "The likeness of the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians is that of a man who hired laborers to work for him until night. The Jews worked until midday, then said: 'We have no need of your wage, and what we have done is in vain.' He then hired others after them and said: 'Complete the rest of your day, and you shall have what I stipulated for them.' So they worked until the time of the 'Asr prayer, then said: 'What we have done is yours in vain, and the wage you set for us is yours.' Then he hired a people to work the rest of their day, and they worked until the sun set, and they received the wage of both groups together. So you are they." Perhaps that prophetic likeness is connected with the allusion to the age of Islam in this verse.

It is also possible to interpret al-'Asr in this verse as all of time. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about al-'Asr, and he said: 'Your Lord has sworn by the end of the day.'" These meanings can be covered by no word other than the word al-'Asr.

The suitability of the oath by al-'Asr to the purpose of the surah, on the reading that the age of Islam is meant, is clear. For the surah explained the condition of people in the age of Islam: between those who disbelieved in it, and those who believed and fully attained their share of the deeds that Islam brought. From it one also learns the condition of those who became Muslims but whose deeds fell short in varying degrees. As for the conditions of the nations before Islam, they differed according to the coming of messengers to some nations, and the remaining of some nations without laws, holding to something other than the religion of Islam, whether polytheism or a religion that Islam came to abrogate (naskh), such as Judaism and Christianity. God Almighty said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, never will it be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The definition of al-insan (mankind) is a generic definition intended to include all (istighraq), and it is a customary inclusion ('urfi),

because it includes the individuals of the human kind present at the time of the revelation of the verse, which is the time of the emergence of Islam, as you have just learned. It is specific to the people whom the call reached in the lands of the world, in varying degrees. Since those who believed and did righteous deeds are excepted from it, its ruling remains in force for non-believers, as will come...

Khusr (loss) is a verbal noun (masdar), the opposite of profit in trade. It is used here metaphorically for the bad outcome of one who thinks that he has a good outcome. That is the lasting outcome, namely the outcome of a human being in his Hereafter, of bliss or punishment.

This has already been discussed at the words of God Almighty: ﴿So their trade did not profit them﴾ [al-Baqara: 16] in Surat al-Baqara. Similar expressions recur in the Qur'an, both near and far.

The containment (zarfiyya) in His words ﴿is in loss﴾ is metaphorical. The constant presence of loss is likened to the enclosure of the container around what it contains, which is more eloquent than saying "Indeed mankind is losing."

The coming of this statement in general terms, together with its confirmation by an oath and by a particle of emphasis in its response, conveys dread and a warning about the state that surrounds most people.

It is followed by the exception in His words: ﴿Except for those who believe﴾ to the end of the verse. Thus the ruling is fully established in the mind of the listener, making clear that people are two groups: a group that is overtaken by loss, and a group that is not touched by any of it. Those who believed and did righteous deeds are not overtaken by loss in any case, provided they did not abandon any righteous deeds by committing their opposites, which are evil deeds.

Among the greatest righteous deeds is repentance from sins for those who commit them. Whoever has the attribute of faith and did not commit evil deeds, or committed them and repented of them, has attained the opposite of loss, which is metaphorical profit, that is, a good outcome of his affair. As for one who did not do righteous deeds and did not repent of his evil deeds, the ruling on that from which the exception is made has been realized in him, namely loss.

This loss varies in degree. The greatest and everlasting is the loss that results from the absence of belief in the oneness of God and the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). Below that, the levels of loss vary according to the abundance of evil deeds, outward and inward. What Islam has defined for this, in terms of the levels of deeds,

and the forgiveness of some minor lapses (lamam) when the one who commits them avoids the major sins and the abominations, is what was given as the interpretation of the words of God Almighty: ﴿Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114].

This statement is meant to take effect in the future, by the indication of the context of warning and threat, that is: in loss in the eternal life of the Hereafter. So no regard is to be given to people's conditions in the life of this world. God Almighty said: ﴿Let not the free movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197].

The indefiniteness (tankir) of (khusr) may be for classification (tanwi'), and it may convey magnification and generality in the context of dread and in the setting of an oath.

The meaning is: people are in great loss, and they are the polytheists.

The definition in His word (al-salihat) is a generic definition intended to include all, that is: they did all the righteous deeds that they were commanded to do by the command of the religion. Doing righteous deeds includes leaving evil deeds. The exception of those described by the content of the relative clause and what is joined to it gives an allusion to the reason for the ruling of the exception, which is the opposite of the ruling established for the one from whom the exception is made. For they are not in loss because they believed and did righteous deeds.

As for faith, it is a reality predicated of its particulars by equivalence (tawatu'). As for righteous deeds, their generality is predicated by gradation (tashkik). This points to the fact that the absence of loss from them is measured by the amount of righteous deeds they did, and in that there are many levels.

The exception of those who believed and did righteous deeds from being in loss indicates that the reason why the rest of mankind is in loss is the absence of faith and righteous deeds, by the indication of the implication of the attribute (mafhum al-sifa). It is known from the relative pronoun that faith and righteous deeds are the cause of the absence of loss enveloping a person.

Mutual advising to truth and mutual advising to patience are joined to doing righteous deeds, even though that is part of doing righteous deeds. This is the joining of the specific to the general for the sake of emphasis, because it may be overlooked, and it may be thought that a righteous deed is what only affects a person's own private conduct. So it alerts us that among the commanded deeds is a Muslim's guiding others and calling them to the truth. Mutual advising to truth includes teaching

the realities of guidance and the beliefs of what is correct, and training the self to understand them by doing what is right and leaving what is wrong.

Mutual advising to patience is joined to mutual advising to truth, again as the joining of the specific to the general, though its specificity is a partial specificity (khusus min wajh), because patience is bearing the hardship of establishing the truth and the harm that confronts a Muslim in his own person in establishing some part of the truth.

The reality of patience is that it is a person's restraining himself from obtaining what he desires, or from attempting to obtain it (if it is hard to obtain), so he gives up attempting to obtain it because of fear of harm arising from taking it, such as fear of God's anger or the punishment of those in authority, or out of desire to gain a benefit from it, such as patience in the hardship of jihad and the Hajj out of desire for reward, and patience in arduous work out of desire to gain wealth or reputation or the like.

Part of patience is bearing what a Muslim meets when he enjoins good, such as the resentment of some of those he enjoins, or their harm by word, like one who says to the one who commands him: "Why don't you look to your own affairs?" or the like.

As for bearing the hardship of doing evil, such as enduring the strain of staying up late in amusement and sins, or enduring the foul taste of wine for its drinker, it is not patience, because that endurance arises from the greater preponderance of the desire for that hardship over the dislike of the hardship that confronts him in abandoning it.
